slide.heading: The Cardiac Cycle
slide.subheading: Pressures, valves, sounds, and the loop that ties them together

lines.text: Happy new year, and welcome to the Spring term. I'm Samuel Adeyemi, cardiology. We start with one heartbeat, taken apart.
Four phases: the ventricle squeezes with its valves shut, ejects, relaxes with its valves shut, and fills.
Everything today, the pressures, the heart sounds, the murmurs, the pressure-volume loop, is the same beat seen from different angles.

slide.heading: Pressures open and close the valves
bullets: Mitral closes (S1): isovolumetric contraction
LV pressure > aortic: aortic valve opens, ejection
LV pressure < aortic: aortic valve closes (S2)
Isovolumetric relaxation, then the mitral opens
Filling: rapid, slow, then the atrial kick

lines.text: Valves are passive. They open and close because of pressure differences, nothing else.

The ventricle starts to contract. As soon as its pressure passes the atrium's, the mitral valve slams shut: the first heart sound. With both valves closed, pressure rises at constant volume: isovolumetric contraction.
When it passes aortic pressure, about eighty here, the aortic valve opens and blood is ejected.
The ventricle relaxes. When its pressure falls below the aorta's, the aortic valve closes: the second heart sound, and the notch on the aortic trace.
Then the mitral valve opens and the ventricle fills: fast at first, then slowly, then a last push from the atrium.

slide.heading: The pressure-volume loop
bullets: Stroke volume = EDV − ESV
Ejection fraction = SV ÷ EDV (normal ≳ 55%)
Width of the loop: stroke volume
Top-left corner: aortic valve closes

series.label: One beat: EDV 120 mL, ESV 50 mL

lines.text: Plot pressure against volume for one beat and you get a loop, run counterclockwise.
The ventricle fills to its end-diastolic volume, here one hundred and twenty millilitres, and ejects down to fifty. The difference is the stroke volume.
Stroke volume over end-diastolic volume is the ejection fraction. Normal is about fifty-five percent or more.
The loop's width is the stroke volume; everything that changes the heart's performance changes the loop's shape.

slide.heading: Heart sounds and murmurs
bullets: S1: mitral and tricuspid close; S2: aortic and pulmonic
Inspiration splits S2 (pulmonic closes later)
S3: early filling of an overfilled ventricle
S4: the atrium pushing into a stiff ventricle
Aortic stenosis: systolic crescendo–decrescendo

lines.text: Put your stethoscope on the chest. S1 is the atrioventricular valves closing; S2, the semilunar valves.
Breathe in, and S2 splits in two. Inspiration increases return to the right heart, so the right ventricle ejects a little longer and the pulmonic valve closes later.
Two extra sounds: an S3, early in diastole, as blood rushes into a big, overfilled ventricle; and an S4, late, as the atrium pushes into a stiff one.
And murmurs are turbulent flow. Aortic stenosis gives a harsh crescendo–decrescendo in systole at the right upper sternal border, radiating to the carotids.

slide.heading: What sets the stroke volume
bullets: Preload: stretch at the end of diastole (EDV)
Frank–Starling: more stretch, stronger beat
Afterload: what the ventricle ejects against
Contractility: the beat's strength at a given stretch

lines.text: Three things set the stroke volume. Preload: how much the ventricle is stretched by the end of filling. Stretch it more, and within limits it beats harder. That's the Frank–Starling law.
Afterload: the pressure it has to eject against. Raise the aortic pressure and the ventricle ejects less, leaving more blood behind.
And contractility: sympathetic stimulation and inotropic drugs shift the whole curve up; a failing heart sits below it.

slide.heading: Summary: one beat, four views
bullets: Valves follow pressure
S1 starts systole; S2 ends it
SV = EDV − ESV; EF = SV ÷ EDV
Preload, afterload, contractility

lines.text: One beat, seen as pressures, sounds and a loop. This afternoon in the ECG lab, you'll see the electrical version.
